extracted.intended_audience: readers of Pascal, students of Christian apologetics and moral theology, general readers interested in philosophical reflections on sin, grace, and human nature
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Pascal's short theological and philosophical aphorisms reflecting on human nature, original sin, grace, prayer, and the proper character of true religion. The page presents evaluative maxims about what constitutes true religion, virtue, and moral conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion tempers fear with hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion 'tempers fear with hope through that double capacity of grace and of sin' and thus humbles without despair and exalts without inflating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion uniquely balances humility and exaltation: it corrects and instructs men better than reason alone because it addresses both their capacity for grace and for sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion must instruct and correct without error
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion alone, being 'exempt from error and vice', fulfils the duty of instructing and correcting men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True religion provides reliable moral instruction where unaided reason fails; this is presented as a criterion for accepting a religion's claim to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of human weakness as central
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is incapable both of complete truth and complete goodness; human weakness is a defining condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging human incapacity for certainty and happiness is presented as necessary moral self-knowledge and as evidence of the need for religion and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire for truth/happiness serves as chastisement and sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Our desire for truth and happiness, combined with our inability to possess them, is left to us partly to punish us and partly to show how far we have fallen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The persistent desire itself is treated as evidence of a fallen state that religion must explain and remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for contradiction: man only happy in God yet opposed to God
rubrics_metrics.description: If man is not made for God, why is he only happy in God? If made for God, why is he so opposed to God?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper religious account must explain both human capacity for divine happiness and human opposition to God; failure to do so marks an inadequate system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption of nature: man does not act by reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Human corruption is shown by the existence of many different and extravagant customs; man often fails to act by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True doctrine should explain the corruption of reason and why truth had to be revealed to pull man beyond himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of true nature, good, virtue, and religion are inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Man's true nature, his true good, true virtue, and true religion are things whose knowledge is inseparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A religion or philosophy that separates these is deficient; an adequate system links anthropology, ethics, and religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater light reveals both greatness and baseness
rubrics_metrics.description: The more light (knowledge) we have, the more greatness and the more baseness we discover in man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An authentic religious explanation deepens knowledge of both human nobility and depravity; mere human wisdom that ignores one side is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original sin is contrary to reason yet superior to human wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Original sin is 'foolishness to men' but 'sapientius est hominibus' — wiser than all human wisdom; reason cannot discover it and is averse to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct religion must include doctrines that may exceed unaided reason and explain why reason resists them; the doctrine of original sin is presented as such a truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural and rabbinic testimony to inherent malignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Various Midrashic and Talmudic passages are cited showing an 'evil leaven' impressed in man's heart from formation, with many scriptural synonyms and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of ancient Jewish sources is offered as corroboration for the doctrine of innate malignity; tradition supports the assessment of human corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-knowledge and desire for deliverance are required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary that those who are in a corrupt state should know it; if we know our faults and do not desire deliverance we are blind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate religious practice both reveals human defects and motivates desire for remedy; absence of either suggests moral blindness or failure of the religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearances of love may conceal lust
rubrics_metrics.description: All men naturally hate one another; they employ lust under pretense of public service — pity or friendship can be compatible with lust and give reputation without real charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral acts by their root motives (love vs. lust), not merely by outward appearances or useful consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/moral rules drawn from selfishness are mere coverings
rubrics_metrics.description: From lust men have extracted excellent rules of policy, morality, and justice, but these only cover the vile root and do not remove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social utility or codified morality that originates in selfish motives does not eliminate the underlying vice; genuine remedy must address the root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self (ego) is unjust and inconvenient even if made socially acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Self has two qualities: it is unjust in itself (centered on itself) and inconvenient to others; removing the inconvenience does not remove the injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral systems should not aim only to mask selfishness's harms; they must address the injustice of self-centeredness itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging nature by self; each believes himself all in all
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person imagines themselves central; we must not judge of nature by ourselves but by its own law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct moral appraisal requires objective standards (e.g., the whole/body analogy), not self-referential judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three orders and three lusts: flesh, spirit, will
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three orders (flesh, spirit, will) and three lusts: 'libido sentiendi, libido sciendi, libido dominandi' — the flesh, the mind, and pride produce different sectarian tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full moral diagnosis recognizes multiple domains of appetite and their distinct corruptions; remedy must address each order appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper seat of pride is wisdom but glory must be given to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride finds its proper place in wisdom, because one cannot claim credit for being made wise; therefore 'Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur' (let him who boasts, boast in the Lord).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility requires acknowledging God as source of true wisdom; pride even in intellectual virtue is disordered unless oriented to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is neither purely within nor without; it is in God
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is neither merely without us (amusement) nor within us (Stoic retreat): 'Happiness is in God, both without us and within us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessories about human flourishing must point to God as the proper end; purely internal or external theories of happiness are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No other religion proposes to hate self; Christianity uniquely does
rubrics_metrics.description: No other religion proposed to men to hate themselves; only Christianity, with the humbled God, answers those inclinations and gives proper objects of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A religion's adequacy is measured by whether it confronts self-love and furnishes a remedy (the humility of God) for those who hate themselves rightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: True religion consists in annihilating self before the Universal Being
rubrics_metrics.description: True religion 'consists in annihilating self before that Universal Being... in recognising that we can do nothing without Him' and in acknowledging our opposition to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious conversion is not civic reform or knowledge acquisition but a reorientation of the will that recognizes dependence on God and need for a mediator.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is unjust to draw others to attach to oneself rather than to God
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not attract persons to attach themselves to me; I ought to warn them to spend their life in pleasing God or seeking Him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral leaders must avoid cultivating personal devotion that distracts from devotion to God; shepherding seeks others' ultimate good, not personal admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renounce self-will to attain contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-will will never be satisfied; we are satisfied the moment we renounce it — without it we cannot be discontented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal spiritual progress involves crucifying self-will; psychological contentment correlates with renunciation of egocentric desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ordering of parts (members) under one will
rubrics_metrics.description: To regulate the love we owe to ourselves, imagine a body full of thinking members: each must submit its particular will to the primary will governing the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social and personal morality requires subordination of individual wills to a higher, harmonious order (analogy to body and soul).

rubrics_metrics.name: Love God only and hate self only
rubrics_metrics.description: We must love God only and hate self only; members must love the body (the whole) because they exist by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion of right love is unity-in-God: self-love is only proper insofar as one loves the whole and ultimately God; all other loves are disordered attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communities should aim at the common whole beyond themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: If members and communities tend to their own welfare, they ought to look to another more general body of which they are members; otherwise self-propensity causes disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and economic orders must be evaluated by how well they orient partial goods to a higher common good, not merely to aggregate self-interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples to imitate must be our members (close ties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of martyrs (our 'members') touch us more and are more formative than examples of strangers or heathens; proximity matters for moral imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral pedagogy should present exemplars who are part of our spiritual community rather than remote figures whose example we cannot internalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two simple laws suffice for Christian polity
rubrics_metrics.description: Two laws are said to suffice to rule the whole Christian Republic better than all statecraft (implied: love God and hate self / love neighbor rightly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity in moral rule is prized: a Christian polity is evaluated by fidelity to fundamental spiritual laws rather than complex civil machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true virtue: hate self and seek the truly lovable (God)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true and only virtue is to hate self (since we are hateful on account of lust) and to seek a truly lovable being to love, which is God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue is measured by reorientation of love away from self toward God; systems that do not inculcate this are deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: A true religion must worship and love one God and teach remedies for human lust
rubrics_metrics.description: Every religion is false if it does not worship one God as origin and love one God as object; the true religion must be aware of human lust and weakness and provide remedies such as prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess religions by whether they command love of one God and provide means (prayer, humility, mortification) to overcome inborn tendencies toward lust and pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: True religion teaches both greatness and misery to produce humility and true greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The true religion must teach greatness and misery; lead to esteem and contempt of self, to love and to hate — balancing humility and loftiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious instruction should avoid unilateral emphases (pure greatness or pure littleness) and present a middle course that cultivates humility without despair and greatness after humiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercy and justice as remedies for pride and sloth
rubrics_metrics.description: God has revealed mercy to combat sloth (exhorting to good works) and justice to humble pride; mercy does not license slackness but attacks sloth by calling to repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological evaluation of moral motivation must hold both humility (via justice) and activity (via mercy) in tension; doctrines that emphasize only one risk producing vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of godliness is due to remaining irreligion; grace combats vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty entering godliness arises from the irreligion that remains in us; suffering in conversion is proportionate to the vice resisting supernatural grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of moral struggle should locate responsibility in the resistances of the world and nature, not in divine action; grace is the enabling remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: External works must be judged by interior disposition and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing so perilous as what pleases God and man because such states have properties pleasing to God and others pleasing to men; manner often matters as much as the thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions not merely by external conformity or social praise but by interior humility and orientation to God; practices that produce self-satisfaction are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral progress: from blame/praise to indifference to praise
rubrics_metrics.description: First step: to be blamed for doing evil, and praised for doing good. Second step: to be neither praised nor blamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiritual maturity is signaled by acting rightly without seeking praise; aim for a state beyond reputational reward or blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as virtues when subordinated to right use
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions, when 'subdued' and employed as slaves by the soul, become virtues; when they become masters they are vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral character by whether passions are regulated by reason/ God-directed will rather than suppressed or celebrated in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just man acts by faith and relies on the Spirit in smallest things
rubrics_metrics.description: The just man acts by faith even in the least things: when he reproves his servants he desires their conversion by the Spirit and prays for God to bless his corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation includes attentiveness to spiritual dependence in action: righteous acts are characterized by prayerful reliance, not merely by efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the broad consequences of even the smallest actions
rubrics_metrics.description: All things can be deadly; 'the least movement affects all nature'; in grace the least action affects everything by its consequences; everything is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by tracing their relational effects (past, present, future) and impacts on others, promoting extreme caution and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace is necessary for sanctity; do not expect it from self
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is indeed needed to turn a man into a saint; hope should not be placed in ourselves but in God; expect nothing from self to receive grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess spiritual progress realistically by acknowledging dependence on divine grace rather than human effort alone; humility in expectation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer: its purposes and divine prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer is established (1) to communicate to creatures the dignity of causality, (2) to teach us from whom our virtue comes, and (3) to make us deserve other virtues by work — yet God grants prayer to whom He pleases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious evaluation of prayer must balance its pedagogical and causal roles with the doctrine of divine election/mercy; do not treat prayer as merely humanly efficacious or automatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boasting excluded; faith not within our power like works of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Romans iii:27: Boasting is excluded; by what law? Not of works but by faith. Faith is not within our power like deeds of the law; it is given otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess spiritual status by exclusion of boasting and recognition of faith as a gift rather than a meritorious achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: True disciples are distinguished by truth making them free
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between disciples and true disciples: the truth will make true disciples free; claiming freedom without evidence of struggle indicates not the true disciple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of spiritual freedom by evidence of truth-led liberty (humility and dependence), not by mere assertion of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law instructs nature; grace gives what law imposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The law imposed what it did not give; grace gives what it imposes. The law instructs, grace makes act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating moral systems, distinguish pedagogical (law) from efficacious (grace) functions: legal obligation without enabling grace is insufficient for true virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach doctrines that prevent both pride and despair
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines should show man's misery (to avoid pride) and God's greatness (to avoid despair); knowledge of Jesus Christ provides the middle course by showing both God and our misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A healthy theological system balances anti-pride and anti-despair motifs, aiming to produce appropriate humility and hope rather than extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater knowledge of duty increases accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: He who knows the will of his master will be beaten with more blows; 'Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc' — greater justification brings greater expectation and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation must weight knowledge and spiritual status: more enlightened persons are held to higher standards and account.
